strengths: Well-motivated, practical problem addressing real C-to-Rust migration challenges
Sensible two-step methodology clearly separating semantic preservation from idiomaticity refinement
Novel FFI-based end-to-end verification approach that is more practical than symbolic execution or fuzz testing
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across two datasets, five LLMs, with detailed cost and failure analysis
Strong empirical results: up to 93% success rate (DeepSeek-R1) with 100% unsafe-free output
Valuable failure categorization providing insights into model-specific strengths (e.g., DeepSeek-R1's robustness on complex code)
Good reproducibility practices with promised code/dataset release and detailed LLM configurations
weaknesses: FUNDAMENTAL ISSUE—Out of scope for ACL: This is a software engineering/systems application paper, not a computational linguistics contribution. It uses LLMs as tools to solve an SE problem but makes no contribution to NLP, language understanding, or LLM capabilities. Should be submitted to ICSE/FSE/ASE instead

Limited evaluation scope: Started with 698/750k+ programs, filtered to 100 total; aggressive filtering for compilation/memory errors likely biases toward easier cases; no justification for 'most LOC' selection criterion

Verification limitations: 'Soft equivalence' via end-to-end tests ≠ functional correctness; relies on test quality; case studies show LLM-generated test harnesses frequently fail; auto-generated tests (CodeNet) not validated

No ablation studies: Why C2Rust only for types? Why exactly 6 retries? Why these static analysis tools? No single-step baseline. No measurement of whether static analysis hints actually improve results

Weak baseline comparison: Baselines have different design goals; Vert only evaluated on one dataset; Figure 7 shows unidiomatic SACTOR already beats all baselines, suggesting improvements from LLM use rather than methodology
Failure categorization lacks rigor: No inter-rater reliability metrics; manual verification after DeepSeek-R1 categorization introduces bias; some category overlaps not addressed; process unclear
Cost analysis incomplete: DeepSeek-R1 costs 5-7× more tokens than GPT-4o but marginal gains not justified; no monetary cost provided; token/query relationship under-explained

Weak real-world generalization: Only 2 case studies; urlparser described as 'simple'; avl_tree has significant failures (10/23 functions); no evidence of scaling to large real-world projects like Linux kernel
Missing statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; LLM variance not analyzed; small post-filtering sample sizes
Limited model analysis: Observes reasoning models perform better but provides no deep investigation into why; no analysis of prompt sensitivity; no few-shot vs. zero-shot comparison
Reproducibility concerns: Closed-source LLMs may change/disappear; no variance analysis across multiple runs; test harness generation failure rate not reported

strengths: Practical and well-motivated problem: C-to-Rust translation with clear real-world value for memory safety
Novel verification approach: FFI-based end-to-end testing is more practical than symbolic execution or fuzz testing for this domain
Comprehensive multi-model evaluation: Tests 5 diverse LLM models with detailed failure categorization revealing model-specific strengths/weaknesses
Well-designed metrics: Idiomaticity metrics (Clippy warnings, unsafe code fraction, unsafe-free fraction) are appropriate and informative
Thoughtful system design: Integration of C2Rust for types, Crown for pointer analysis, and custom C parser demonstrates good engineering
Detailed documentation: Extensive appendices with dataset descriptions, prompts, and configurations aid reproducibility and understanding
weaknesses: Fundamental venue mismatch: This is a software engineering systems paper with no computational linguistics or NLP contribution; inappropriate for ACL. Should be submitted to ICSE, ISSTA, or ASE instead

Limited verification guarantees: 'Soft equivalence' via end-to-end tests only validates behavior on specific test cases, not semantic correctness. No formal memory safety guarantees despite Rust's core value proposition

Circular evaluation on CodeNet: Tests were auto-generated for a dataset without end-to-end tests, making validation circular. Uses generated tests to validate the very tool that would be used—undermines the 84% claim

Unfair baseline comparisons: SACTOR uses 6 attempts with feedback; baselines run once. No ablation isolating the two-step approach, static analysis hints, or feedback mechanism. No comparison with vanilla LLM prompting

Dataset selection bias: Removed 'buggy programs' and filtered for specific input patterns (argc/argv), removing edge cases where translation is most challenging. N=100 per dataset is small with no statistical significance testing
Reproducibility failure: Code and datasets stated as 'available at [blank]'—not provided for review. This is disqualifying for any research venue

Missing ablation studies: No isolation of key components (Crown, static analysis hints, feedback loops). Success may be primarily due to detailed prompt engineering (Appendix F) rather than methodology

Limited scope and known failures: Cannot handle random number generation or mutable global state (S4, S5). Case studies show only 10/23 functions successfully translated. Idiomatic translation fails on complex data conversions and function pointers
Overstated idiomaticity claims: 100% unsafe-free fraction only counts successful translations. The 16-22% failures have unknown safety profiles. Metric choice favors successful cases
Incomplete cost analysis: DeepSeek-R1 consumes 5-7× more tokens for modest success improvements (93% vs 83-90%). No cost-benefit analysis vs alternatives or deployment feasibility discussion

Methodological concerns: Test harness generation works only for simple types and fails on complex data structures. No statistics on harness success rates. FFI compatibility requirements may introduce their own bugs
Weak failure analysis: Manual categorization of ~100 failures; claims like 'reasoning models better' based on DeepSeek-R1 alone lack statistical backing
Missing statistical rigor: No confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. No cross-validation or multiple runs. Differences (e.g., 78% vs 84%) lack statistical validation

strengths: Well-motivated, practical problem with clear security/safety benefits for C-to-Rust migration
Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 200+ programs, 5 LLMs, multiple datasets, detailed failure analysis with categorization
Sound two-step methodology: unidiomatic (semantic preservation) → idiomatic (safety/idiomaticity) is principled problem decomposition
Novel FFI-based end-to-end verification approach is more practical for real-world code than symbolic execution/fuzz testing
Strong empirical results: 93% success rate (DeepSeek-R1), 100% unsafe-free translations, outperforms 4 baselines on idiomaticity
Valuable insight that reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1) outperform on complex code with intricate logic/arrays
Practical cost analysis (token consumption, query counts) provides actionable guidance
Clear presentation with effective figures, examples, and comprehensive appendices
weaknesses: Limited scope for ACL (computational linguistics): This is a software engineering paper; does not advance NLP/LLM methodology or theory, better suited for ICSE/PLDI/ASE
Not genuinely 'zero-shot': Heavily dependent on static analysis tools (libclang, C2Rust, Crown); hybrid neuro-symbolic approach obscures independent LLM contribution; missing ablation studies
Limited novelty in LLM methodology: Standard prompting techniques (context, dependencies, error feedback); no insights into code understanding or novel prompting strategies

Verification limitations: 'Soft equivalence' (E2E test success) is not comprehensive correctness guarantee; CodeNet test generator details largely absent; unresolved challenges in case studies (function pointers, harness generation)

Dataset/sampling concerns: TransCoder-IR selects only longest 100/698 programs (potential bias); CodeNet only 100/750k+ with restrictive filtering; real-world evaluation: only 2 projects insufficient for generalization
Missing ablation studies: No quantitative assessment of C2Rust vs. Crown vs. LLM contributions independently; single-stage vs. two-stage comparison absent
Insufficient statistical rigor: No confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance reporting; only one run per program; small real-world sample
Cost-performance tradeoff unaddressed: DeepSeek-R1 requires 5-7× more tokens than GPT-4o; cost analysis excludes failed attempts (biased)
Missing implementation details: SACTOR test generator for CodeNet (creation/validation methodology), adaptive prompting rules, C Parser design/limitations underexplained
Reproducibility concerns: Code/dataset URLs redacted; LLM versions change over time; inherent challenges with LLM-based research reproducibility not fully addressed

strengths: Two-stage pipeline elegantly separates semantic preservation from idiomatic refinement, providing a generalizable design pattern for code transformation
Comprehensive evaluation across 200+ programs and real-world codebases (CRust-Bench, libogg) with 6 LLM models and detailed failure categorization (5-7 categories per dataset)
Significant idiomaticity improvements: 100% unsafe-free translations vs 0-45.6% for baselines; 0.28 avg Clippy alerts/function vs 1.60-2.96 for rule-based methods
Pragmatic FFI-based E2E verification with SPEC-driven harness generation avoids infeasible symbolic execution while enabling practical validation
Strong integration of static analysis (C2Rust, Crown, custom C Parser) to guide LLM prompts, with ablation studies demonstrating 17% contribution from Crown
Honest assessment of limitations including test coverage dependence, model variance, unsupported C features, and harness generation stability
weaknesses: Fundamental scope mismatch: This is a software engineering/program synthesis paper, not a computational linguistics or NLP contribution. Venue should be ICSE/FSE/ASE, not ACL.

Overstated correctness claims: 'Soft equivalence' via E2E testing cannot guarantee formal correctness. Untested paths may contain bugs; C undefined behavior and Rust safety gaps create undetectable mismatches.
Moderate real-world performance: CRust-Bench shows only 25% fully idiomatic (8/32 samples); libogg 53-78% idiomatic success. Majority of translations require manual intervention for production use.

Statistical rigor absent: No confidence intervals, significance tests, or single-pass success rates (6 retries inflates reported success); trivial baseline gets 10 attempts vs SACTOR's 6, unfairly favoring SACTOR.

Reproducibility compromised: Code repository link incomplete; proprietary LLM dependency (GPT-4o/GPT-5); CRust-Bench from 2025 (unstable); SPEC/harness implementation details scattered across appendices.

Soft equivalence limitations underexplored: E2E testing provides no coverage guarantees; Table 14 shows many runtime/compile failures despite 'passing' translations, indicating false positives in verification.

strengths: Comprehensive evaluation across 4 datasets and 6 LLM models with detailed failure analysis
Practical engineering: FFI-based end-to-end verification is clever for mixed-language correctness checking
Two-stage pipeline (unidiomatic → idiomatic) is well-motivated and sensible decomposition
Extensive appendices with ablation studies, prompts, per-sample outcomes, and honest limitation discussion
Real-world evaluation on libogg library (77 functions) and CRust-Bench shows attempt at realistic assessment
weaknesses: Fundamental scope mismatch: This is a systems/software engineering paper, not an NLP/CL contribution. No advances to understanding language translation or linguistics. Belongs at ICSE/PLDI, not ACL

Evaluation methodology flawed: Up to 6 attempts per translation inflates success rates; unfair vs baselines; soft equivalence (test-based verification only) is weak; dataset filtering limits generalization
Real-world performance is weak: 52% idiomatic success on CRust-Bench (harder real code) vs 80-93% on synthetic benchmarks; 22-41 functions still fail on libogg despite guidance from static analysis

Limited novelty: Primarily orchestrates existing tools (C2Rust, Crown); two-stage pipeline is intuitive engineering, not algorithmic innovation; SPEC-driven harness covers only 10 patterns with many LLM fallbacks
Baseline comparisons insufficient: Idiomaticity metrics only on TransCoder-IR; no head-to-head correctness comparisons on same programs; trivial baseline (Table 9) uses unfair attempt budgets

Failure analysis reveals fundamental issues not edge cases: symbol naming drift (15+ CRust-Bench samples), function pointers, C variadics, global state—these are common C idioms the approach cannot handle
Cost analysis underemphasized: DeepSeek-R1 uses 5-7× more tokens than GPT-4o; practical deployment cost for migrations not analyzed; reproducibility compromised by proprietary LLM dependency

CRust-Bench evaluation bottleneck: Only 32/50 samples pass unidiomatic stage (64%), further reducing idiomatic evaluation to 8/32 (25% of original 50); dataset filtering excludes circular dependencies and intrinsics
Circular dependency handling unsupported: Treated as fatal error despite being common in real C code (doubly-linked lists); significant architectural limitation
Pointer analysis precision: 17% drop in performance without Crown (Table 10) suggests fundamental imprecision in ownership/fatness inference; approach heavily dependent on external tool correctness

strengths: Well-motivated two-stage pipeline that elegantly separates semantic preservation from idiomatic refinement, with solid justification for the decomposition
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple datasets (200+ programs) and six LLM models with detailed failure categorization and ablation studies
Practical FFI-based verification strategy that reuses existing test suites and is more scalable than symbolic execution or fuzzing
Thoughtful system design integrating existing tools (C2Rust, Crown, custom parser) with novel SPEC-driven harness generation using rule-based + LLM fallback
Strong results on synthetic benchmarks (93-94% unidiomatic, 80-93% idiomatic) with transparent acknowledgment of test-coverage dependence
Valuable insights from failure analysis showing how different LLM architectures struggle with specific issues (e.g., Claude with strings, DeepSeek-R1 with complex bugs)
Excellent reproducibility: detailed prompts, configurations, ablations, and code/dataset release promised
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty—contribution is primarily in engineering orchestration of existing techniques (LLM prompting, static analysis, E2E testing) rather than new methods

Modest performance on real-world code (52% idiomatic on CRust-Bench, 25% full-sample success) substantially lags synthetic benchmarks (93-94%), limiting practical applicability for complete migrations
Heavy dependence on specific LLM capabilities creates sustainability concerns; performance varies significantly across models and will likely become obsolete with new generations

Significant unsupported C features (variadics, complex macros, pervasive function pointers, global state) are common in real-world code, limiting scope; applicability constraints not clearly stated upfront
Correctness verification relies entirely on test coverage ('soft equivalence'); no analysis of how often bugs escape when tests are incomplete or shallow—concerning for safety-critical code
Baseline comparisons somewhat unfair: non-LLM baselines (C2Rust, Crown) vs. LLM-based approach; only Vert comparison is direct, and limited to one dataset
Harness generation remains a bottleneck despite SPEC approach—17 libogg failures due to harness issues; complex patterns require LLM fallback with uncertain robustness
Prompt engineering brittle and model-dependent; unclear how well approach generalizes across LLM families or how to adapt as new models emerge
Statistical rigor lacking: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; success rate variations across attempts not clearly explained
Real-world applicability unclear: no analysis of how much partially-translated code can be salvaged, no user studies on generated code quality, and substantial manual review needed
